text: or establish appropriate liability, we should welcome it, embracing the critical roles of states not only to protect consumers, but be the laboratory of democracy. Right now, the FTC, FCC, and CFPB risk being cops off of their beat, and Congress must empower them, resource them, and restore them in order to aggressively protect consumers. The American people deserve nothing less. Thanks again for the opportunity to testify, and I'm happy to answer any questions you might have.

I thank you all for your testimony. We will now move on to questioning. I will begin and recognize myself for 5 minutes. Mr. Bercu, the Broadband Association's Industry Traceback Group conducted more than 3,600 tracebacks of suspected unlawful robocalls in 2024. Generally speaking, what percentage of unlawful robocalls are foreign-originated?

Thank you for the question. So I don't have an exact number on, on how many came from foreign foreign countries or foreign entities, but we do know that a lot of the fraud does come from abroad. Illegal telemarketing, we see that sometimes originate at home, sometimes abroad, but a lot of the fraud does originate overseas. And one of the things we've been seeing a lot lately is because so much of enforcement and regulation was focused on who brought the illegal call into the country, what we're now seeing is some of the bad actors spinning out U.S.-based LLCs so that we're tracing it to a U.S. entity, that probably has no, no people in the United States at all.

Do we— dealing with the foreign actors, though, that creates some tremendous challenges because we can't charge them with a crime right now unless they're operating in-country. Is there any recourse through civil action? I mean, what, what recourse do you have to deal with foreign actors? And be as brief as you can.

Yeah, I think we can do criminal action, and I think that needs to be a priority. The same people attacking us here are attacking other countries as well. I think there's a lot of opportunities for collaboration, and just to give you one anecdote, when the FBI did work several years ago with the Central Bureau of Intelligence in India to raid some of the call centers there, we saw IRS robocalls drop 80% overnight.
Ms. Leggin, can you tell us how CTIA's Secure Messaging Initiative works to trace back robotexts, and how effective has this been to to stop illegal and unwanted robotexts?

Thank you for the question. CTIA's Secure Messaging Initiative was launched to convene the messaging ecosystem and the various players that have a role there in protecting consumers, so that we can facilitate information sharing among the industry stakeholders to complement their existing industry tools to better fight the bad actors, and then to share that information with law enforcement partners at the FCC, FTC, DOJ, and the 50-State Attorney General Enforcement Task Force. To date, we've done over 172,000 robotexts as part of those information packages that we share with law enforcement. And we've done over a dozen of those packages that focus on scams that you all have seen, including government or bank impersonation, package delivery, and AI-enhanced scams as well. We continue to focus on the areas where we're hearing that scams are happening for consumers so that we give that information to law enforcement so they can prioritize their efforts to go after the bad actors and stop the traffic at the source.
Mr. Bercu, I want to go back to you. How widely has the STIR/SHAKEN caller ID authentication framework been implemented, and what percentage of the providers still need to implement the framework?

So under FCC rules, it's implemented on the IP portions of providers' networks, and we've seen a shift in practice because of, especially, the high-volume illegal telemarketers. One of the things—they, I think because of STIR/SHAKEN, have moved away from spoofing to actually getting real numbers, which STIR/SHAKEN doesn't directly address.

Okay. Mr. Waguespack, in your testimony, you were talking about how the private right of action has been abused, and it's been abused instead of protecting people who have been harmed by scam robocalls. It's led to basically a cottage industry that's attacking legitimate companies. Can you talk a little bit about that?

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Well, in the opening statements from the panel and obviously from the witnesses here, there seems to be a unified focus that these bad actors, a lot of times which are very hard to find, which are located overseas, those are the true ones driving a lot of this issue. The private right of action provisions within TCPA are not utilized to go after those bad actors. Instead, a cottage industry has developed to go after simply where there's opportunities to make money. And also, the provisions of the PRA within TCPA are extremely broad compared to other federal statutes. There's no cap— there's no caps on recovery as you see in HIPAA, no safe harbor provision you see in COPPA, no cap on attorney fees as you see in other statutes. And so it's created a class action factory that's being exploited by just a handful of firms and a lot
of those kind of— use of the private right of action. I saw where one of the judgments was for $260-something million. So how do we respond to that?

I think we borrow from other statutes already in place at the federal level. You look to HIPAA to put a cap on the total recovery. They set that at $25,000. There's no cap here. It's up to $15,000 per occurrence under this statute, which absolutely drives those numbers up. And most of these suits, they're not trying to win in court. They're just trying to drive discovery, to make it very expensive and drive settlement. And you're seeing it play out time and time again. In fact, there is one law firm that has done over 155 cases over a three-year period on this front. They've developed a niche market. There is even one plaintiff who has done almost 125 himself on this issue. So you have a handful of folks exploiting this system. That is not helping the consumers that desperately need some of the help from these scam robocalls.
Thank you. The chair now recognizes the ranking member of the subcommittee, Ms. Clarke, for 5 minutes for her questions.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Unwanted calls continue to be the top consumer complaint received by the FCC, the Federal Communications Commission. In 2024, Americans received over 52 billion robocalls, and 49% of those robocalls were scams or from telemarketers. Mr. Bercu, how has the robocall and robotext threat landscape changed since the implementation of the TRACED Act and STIR/SHAKEN?

So I think we, we've made a lot of progress, but as you're recognizing, there's, there's work left to do. We have seen complaints. They're still too high, but they've dropped pretty dramatically from the highs from several years ago. We've seen some of the bad actors instead of for scam robocalls, there's some day they're about 50% of what they once were for scam robocalls. But we've seen the scammers move from mass robocalls to more targeted, more sophisticated attacks where they know who exactly who they're calling. So that's a little bit of how this has changed over time.

Thank you. So we still have more to do. With the work left undone in the fight against phone scams, it baffles me that the Trump administration is undermining the government institutions that combat them. In March, President Trump attempted to illegally remove Senate-confirmed commissioners from the Federal Trade Commission, an independent agency with the explicit mission to protect the public from unfair and deceptive business practices like unlawful telemarketing and robocalls. And in April, in accordance with the Trump administration instruction, the Department of Justice announced plans to dissolve its Consumer Protection Branch, which tries cases targeting large-scale scams against seniors, AI and cybercrimes against consumers, and illegal telemarketing. This just makes no sense. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, FCC, FTC, and the Department of Justice have all been hit by early retirements, terminations, and deferred resignations, and they are all agencies that combat the robocall problem we are gathered to discuss today. Mr. Winters, how does an unstable and depleted FCC and FTC workforce impact the role both agencies play in addressing the robocall scams?

Thanks for the question. Um, I mean, a under-resourced— these under-resourced consumer protection agencies is just a big win for scammers, right? Uh, less cops on the beat mean less consequences, and, uh, they can sort of act with impunity. And so, uh, what we need to be doing, and I think was reflected in, uh, all of our testimony today, is that we need more enforcement. More resources and more proactive behavior. And everything about— from firing commissioners to budget cuts goes exactly against that.

Thank you. Last week, President Trump released a detailed fiscal year 2026 funding proposal. If enacted, this proposal would make permanent and add to the number of fired federal employees, including 74 at the FCC, 83 at the FTC, and 32 of which are identified as consumer protection roles. The proposal also cuts $42 million from the FTC, and more than $18 million of which would go directly toward protecting consumers. Mr. Winters, what would happen to the robocall-fighting infrastructure if the federal government pulled back from its role, whether it be from a lack of manpower, funds, or general disinterest in holding scammers accountable?
Uh, in the interest of time, I'll be simple in that it will get worse.

And what do the government actions we have discussed today tell the scammers and fraudsters who conduct robocalls and texts about the priorities of the U.S. government? Do you think actions like these make robocalls more likely to occur in the future?

Yeah, I mean, I think, uh, it incentivizes bad behavior. It makes people feel like we are absolutely not going to be able to— uh, we're not going to get enforcement action against us. Uh, it's going to be hard to track. It's hard to track when you have a full-court press against it, and we've seen that for years. But if we're pulling back, then that's even, you know, an unimaginable harm for American consumers.

Very well. Well, Mr. Chairman, in their written testimony, several of today's witnesses said Congress must increase support for and prioritize enforcement actions if we truly want to stop bad actors. The experts are calling for more funding and enforcement, not less. And I ask my colleagues across the aisle to listen to them. With that, I yield back.
Thank you, Mrs. Clarke. Next is Chairman of the full committee, Mr. Guthrie.

Thank you. I thank all the witnesses for being here. I appreciate y'all being here this morning. So, Mr. Bercu, in July 2020, the FCC first selected USTelecom—The Broadband Association's Industry Traceback Group as the single registered consortium to conduct private-led traceback efforts and has redesignated USTelecom's ITG each year since. So could you kind of explain—I know I'm going between two hearings, so if you're repetitive, it helps me to repeat anyway. So how does traceback work, and how has the USTelecom ITG helped the FCC with its efforts to fight illegal robocalls?

Yeah, absolutely. So, traceback helps solve for one of the problems, which was when a call is spoofed and we don't know where it's coming from, the carrier doesn't know exactly where it came from. STIR/SHAKEN helps with that, but traceback goes even farther. And we go hop by hop in a semi-automated system through a portal, and we find out exactly where it's coming from. And in fact, in our tracebacks, we've identified over 2,000 providers from 75 different countries. So, we'll trace it all over the world until we can find out who's making the calls and actually disrupt it there. Our data has been used for virtually every robocall enforcement by the FCC, by the FTC, by the state AGs. So, it's been a very successful partnership with the industry and government.

Shouldn't the technology be in place, let's say if I'm sitting in Bowling Green, Kentucky, and a phone call is coming from Nigeria that's not in my data in my cell phone or anything like that, should that be blocked? There's technology that can block that from coming. You have to sign up for it, I gather, but there's technology that keeps that from coming to your phone, doesn't there?

The challenge is that there's not perfect information at the carrier side about where that call is coming from. STIR/SHAKEN helps with that. I'm optimistic that a recent rule clarification the FCC did last year, that will continue to advance STIR/SHAKEN and the impact there. But that's the challenge, and so there's definitely tools to achieve that, but the carriers don't have perfect information and know that call was coming from Nigeria.

My understanding is that when a lot of these robocalls happen, they're not like I'm calling Neal Dunn in Florida and faking him out or something, I'm like I'm a criminal in Bowling Green calling Neal Dunn in Florida. It's usually spam is just thousands of calls instantaneously going out. Can carriers not determine that and block those calls?

So that type, it still happens, but that's at a fraction of what it once was thanks to enforcement, thanks to the TRACED Act, thanks to STIR/SHAKEN. Those types of calls are down, depending on the day you look, about 50%. Where we've seen fraud calls, a lot of the robocalls that people still hate, a lot of those are illegal telemarketing. That's the majority of the robocalls people get where it's telemarketing that no one consented to and they're violating the TCPA. But what we're seeing with the scams are the scams are getting more sophisticated, more targeted, where they are targeting individuals.
Okay. So, Ms. Leggin, could you talk about how the CTIA is trying to fight help fight these spam calls and robocalls?
Sure thing. Thank you for the question. Um, as Josh said, um, I think
you probably need your mic. I know, though. There you go.
Try that again?
Yeah, perfect. It was on.
Is it on now?
Maybe just closer to it. Yeah, closer to it.

Sorry, can't see if it's on or not. Thank you for the question. Like Josh's members, the wireless industry are dedicated to protecting consumers from illegal and unwanted robocalls. We helped lead the way in developing the STIR/SHAKEN framework, and we supported this committee's efforts through the TRACED Act to promote the deployment of that. And it's now working well as a call authentication tool to help protect consumers from spoofed calls. It's just one tool in the toolbox, though. So especially over the last few years, we've been developing lots of different call blocking, labeling, filtering tools to complement STIR/SHAKEN as part of a multi-pronged approach to protect consumers from robocalls. At CTIA, we're developing the next generation of call authentication, which is branded calling, or CTIA's BCID, or Branded Calling ID, which gives consumers even more information about who is calling and why to help empower consumers about whether to answer the phone again, as well as protecting them by providing consumer resources that educate them about which calls to ignore, so that we are kind of coming at it from all fronts.

I assume that could be a competitive thing between providers to say, Hey, if you use our service, we can help you block your robocalls. I think that would be— So, Mr. Waguespack, how about increasing fines for illegal robocalls? Would such a change affect legitimate businesses? And how can we improve collection of existing fines or overall enforcement?

My phone just spoke, ironically. Obviously, FCC and FTC, I think, have done a really great job working with industry partners to develop, through traceback and other initiatives, to identify those. So we definitely encourage strong enforcement and add that DOJ should also go after these bad actors any way we can. We think going through those channels, as compared to unleashing a small niche cadre of plaintiff firms to go after, quite frankly, credible businesses just because they can't find the bad actors, has been the wrong, minor approach within TCPA. So it's that private right of action that truly, we think, is a disincentive to businesses to reach out to develop those partnerships with their consumers that, quite frankly, most of their consumers want.
Okay, thank you. Well, my time's expired and I'll yield back. Appreciate you all being here. Thanks.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Next up is the ranking member of the full committee, Mr. Pallone.

speaker_label: Full Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
text: Thank you so much. And look, I think we all know we have to do more to stop these dangerous and unwanted calls and texts that continue to bombard Americans. I mean, I get so many myself every day, and they're not just harassment, they're causing real harms. The phone scams alone defrauded Americans of $25 billion in 2023. Now, the TRACED Act, which I authored in 2019, required the implementation of the STIR/SHAKEN call authentication technology to help verify the legitimacy of calls. So I want to ask Mr. Barron— no, I'm sorry, Bercu, you run the Industry Traceback Group, which traces calls to their origin as required by the TRACED Act on behalf of the communications industry. In your testimony, you discuss how industry is utilizing this framework to fight the problem of robocalls and to protect consumers from scam artists. What more can industry do to protect consumers from unwanted and dangerous robocalls and robotexts? I'm going to ask you a question and then Mr. Winters, so, a couple minutes.

Sure. So, thank you for the question, Ranking Member Pallone. I think the industry—we do have blocking and labeling deployed. STIR/SHAKEN is deployed. I think there's a lot of work there, but I think what our experience shows is that when we're dealing with whether it's the illegal telemarketers, whether it's the criminal fraudsters abroad, they don't stop because it gets a little bit harder. This is their business, so they keep trying to find new paths. So I think what we see with traceback, we are tracing them back. We've adapted to tracing back the targeted scam calls, working closely with the financial sector, other sectors as well. I think that's more of the work to be done, complemented by very aggressive enforcement against the actual bad actors.

speaker_label: Full Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
text: Now thank you. So, in March, President Trump illegally, in my opinion, fired the two Democratic FTC commissioners, meaning that their crucial voices are missing from any discussion at FTC of how to better protect consumers from robocalls and robotexts. And they have my full support in their ongoing lawsuit to be rightfully restored at the FTC, and I think that's the very first step that needs to be taken. But just last year, I introduced, and I mentioned also, the Do Not Disturb Act, a comprehensive piece of legislation that aims to build on the success of the TRACED Act, and it would ensure that scam artists using illegal robocalls or robotexts can't explain— can't exploit new loopholes as new technology makes it even easier for fraudsters to steal from Americans. So, Mr. Winters, I have two questions. You've got 2 minutes. Do you agree there's a need for legislation to provide update to current laws like last year's Do Not Disturb Act? And do the FTC and FCC need more authority from Congress to fight text message scams? Is it just money and enforcement, or they actually need more authority, if you will?

Thank you. Yeah. So on that first question, I think there's a lot more that Congress can do, and there's there's more that they need to do. And so whether that is some of the provisions in the Do Not Disturb Act, like codifying the rule about AI disclosures and increasing penalties for AI-generated scam calls, there is a lot more that can be done by Congress, including giving more resources to not just the FCC, but to state attorneys general, who are leading the forefront of a lot of this work, and increasing collaboration like

speaker_label: Full Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
text: But do they need more authority, though?

They do need more authority. One thing in particular is that they're not able to directly collect fines. They have to refer fine collection to the Department of Justice, and so they have to rely on another overworked agency to collect fines. And we see a lot of times, although there are big headlines and numbers of fines, the FCC might not actually be able to resolve and get a lot of that money back. So that's one thing that needs to be done in terms of authority. And they also need the authority to put more automatic suspension and provisions in the Robocall Mitigation Database, so that when there are repeat bad actors, they are automatically taken out. They can't just stay in the Robocall Mitigation Database. There is not enough sort of continued standards and continued enforcement using that.

speaker_label: Full Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone (D-NJ)
text: Well, thank you. And, Mr. Chairman, as you can see, I think there's a question of more more authority that's needed for the agencies. But I'll repeat what I said earlier, which is they also need more resources and staff. And cutting back on staff and firing some of the commissioners is certainly not the way to go if you really want to try to improve the situation with robocalls. And so, I would not only ask that we try to move towards more authority to fight these scams, but also provide the resources, not cut the resource, not cut the staff. And with that, I'll yield back.

Thank you, Mr. Pallone. I am up next, so welcome, everybody. I'm glad you were able to join us. Ms. Leggin, I will direct my questions to you this morning. According to the FCC, text message scams have increased 500-fold in recent years. How have scams become more sophisticated over the years?

Thanks for the question. CTIA and our members are dedicated to protecting consumers from scam and spam text messages, while also making sure that legitimate ones go through, because we know that consumers open and read and trust their text messages as one of the most preferred platforms for communications today. Over the years, we have seen bad actors increasingly target text messaging because they know that consumers open and read those texts. So, as bad actors have evolved and enhanced their tactics, we've evolved and enhanced our defenses as well. So, over the years, we've enhanced our blocking, filtering tools by enhancing them with machine learning and AI. We've launched the Secure Messaging Initiative, which is our work to partner with law enforcement to give them actionable information about bad actors so that they can go and take traffic off at the source. And those are working to help the FCC, the FTC, DOJ, and the attorneys general enforcement task force in giving them information they can go after bad actors with.
Okay. Thank you very much. You also answered my follow-up. Are mobile carriers and other industry players doing enough to address the growth in scam and illegal robotechs?

Our industry is really dedicated to this issue. Um, as just one metric, we've blocked over 55 billion texts last year while also making sure that the legitimate ones go through and supporting over 2 trillion, uh, legitimate texts. So it really is always a balance, but we've dedicated a lot of different resources to, um, enhancing our protections against bad actors. Um, In terms of more things we can do, again, we welcome help from Congress in prioritizing resources towards enforcement so that the agencies we work with can take on more of those cases, do more investigations, and go after the bad actors to stop that traffic at the source.

All right. Thank you. How well are mobile carriers engaging with states and other entities for information sharing and enforcement? For example, with the scam toll texts, did mobile carriers pause delivery and contact state toll authorities to verify the legitimacy of the numbers?

Our members were focused on the toll road scams as well as the other versions of that as part of our work to protect consumers from all those types of scams that impersonate legitimate businesses. The wireless carriers, as well as other partners in the messaging ecosystem, including providers of other types of messaging apps that were targeted by that type of scam, including over-the-top, online-based, and app-based messaging, all were working together to share information with law enforcement. To help them find the bad actors responsible and take them off the field.

Okay. Thank you. How can we get mobile carriers to better engage and pull their weight to stop the flood of robotechs at the same levels robocalls— at the same level they did for robocalls? I'm sorry.

The wireless industry and our messaging ecosystem partners are really focused on this issue. For years, we have been seeing bad actors really target the voice network because there were not blocking and other protections in place until the last few years. In text messaging, we've actually had the ability to block and to filter and to employ upfront vetting and verification for decades. And so, for a long time, the messaging platform was really protected from bad actors. Of course, bad actors are getting more sophisticated and over the last few years targeting text messaging more. But this has been an area of focus and a priority for our members for years, and we continue to dedicate significant resources toward protecting consumers while maintaining trust in text messaging.
Okay, thank you very much. I yield back my remaining time. Next up is the gentlelady from Colorado, Ms. DeGette.

Thank you so much. So I just got back, along with many of our colleagues on this committee, from a conference on artificial intelligence, and so I'd like to talk with you about that today because I think it's really being implemented in a disturbing way by scammers to find new ways to deal with Americans. A lot of us have been hearing these chilling stories about how somebody gets called by somebody who they think is their child or their parent and asked for money, and the voice sounds eerily like their loved one. So, Mr. Winters, I want to ask you, how has AI technology been used to create more sophisticated robocall and robotext scams that target consumers?

Thanks for the question. It's been in a lot of different ways, and so I'll categorize the two different types of AI systems in it. So one, in text generation services, like sort of I mentioned in my opening statement, whether it's something like ChatGPT or Claude that you might have played around with or one of the one that even has less moderation, you can create a bunch of texts really quickly that have good grammar and seems like you don't have the bells going off in your head from them. So you can do that. You can have lists of people's names, target based off their location, other information you have, have it connect to a link of a wallet or a Zelle or something like that. So it's just a sort of scale and accuracy and plausibility thing. The other big category is the sort of impersonation of people, whether that be through voice or video, and that's where you see the really harrowing stories of sort of like real-time fraud and deepfake stuff that have not only caused a lot of emotional harm, but have sort of ruined people's lives. Yeah.
Yeah, so this kind of goes without saying, but because of this degree of sophistication, even when you have an educated consumer, it becomes much more difficult to identify these scams.

Absolutely. I think that one thing is it's really difficult and kind of an impossible proposition to have all American people be able to spot when something is AI in the moment and then not respond to the emotional sort of I'm your son and I'm in jail thing even if you do or are able to flag that. And then all not all AI-generated anything will be a scam or a fraud. So it's complicated there because you don't necessarily want to teach that. It will just get people paranoid. So it is really it should be on the companies and on the
Right. So if we're not going to rely on the on the consumers by education, Ms. Leggin, what more can industry do to filter these messages and prevent them from ever getting to the victims?

So as Mr. Winters said, it is a balanced approach to make sure that we are blocking the messages that we don't want consumers to receive and they don't want to receive, while also making sure that legitimate ones go through.
That's right.

So, with AI-enhanced scams, for example, there are aspects of that that we can also detect using AI by analyzing vaster quantities of data, by enhancing our existing tools and algorithms and frameworks, and then by complementing those with large fraud teams to help protect consumers from scams.
And do you think that that the federal agencies have the necessary authorities to fight against these scams, or can companies do it themselves? Do they have the authority to do it?
We value our partnerships with all the law enforcement entities, including the FCC, FTC,
Right. Do you think they have enough authority to do it?
We think—
yes or no will work.
We think that the best authority, the best way for them to continue to help us is by prioritizing resources towards enforcement.
resources. So that means Congress and the administration have to adequately fund them, right?
We continue to work on
that. No, no, yes or no will work.
Yes.
Okay. Mr. Winters, do you think they have enough authority?
No.
And why is that?

I mean, if they did and they had the resources as well, I think we probably would not be here today. You know, they need an ability to, as I mentioned, follow up on the fines that they levy and actually collect those. They need sort of required transparency and basic moderation challenges, obligations for AI companies. There are lots of things that just using something like unfair deceptive practices authority are— Okay,

Thanks. We look forward to working with you to see what new authorities we want. I just have a little time left, so I want to ask you one more question. In the bill, the great big bill a couple of weeks ago that we're now learning all of the things that were included, one of the thing that was included in the reconciliation package was a 10-year moratorium on state and local enforcement of their own AI bills. Does a 10-year moratorium on state AI bills prevent states from using evolving technologies to help fight this program? And do you think that's something Congress should look at, look at, Mr. Winters?
Um, so we vehemently oppose the moratorium provision. I don't think the moratorium as written would stop state agencies from using AI, but it would harm consumers without a doubt.
Thank you. I yield back.
Thank you. Next up is my good friend Mr. Griffith from Virginia.

Let me start in a little bit different direction than I planned on going. Ms. Leggin, you were asked about adequate funding a minute ago, and I got the sense that while you were told to give a yes-or-no answer, you want to see the Federal Trade Commission and others receive adequate funding, but it seemed to me that you were not trying to get into the debate as to what the definition of adequate funding is. Am I correct that that I read your body language correctly, that you didn't want to get into that debate, but you do want them to be adequately funded?

That's right. It's up to each agency to allocate resources to their enforcement teams, but what we've said is, and what we're seeing with our work with our enforcement partners, is that sometimes the consumer fraud protection folks lack the personnel or resources they need to go after cases. So we welcome, you know, information collection or just a way to try to allocate the existing resources.
But it's also true that AI may make this much more efficient. And so we're looking forward to that, too. Is that not correct?
That's right.

I got to move on to what I really was going to go after, both for you, you and Mr. Bercu. The good news is is that the fraud, while terrible, is on the downward slope, and I hear from my constituents all the time about receiving robocalls. And a couple of years ago, it was all about the fraudulent stuff and they were concerned about that. But I will tell you, in the last year, particularly in the last few months, the real concern has become Medicare, and particularly Medicare Advantage solicitors calling up the folks in my district. And I have an older population, generally speaking, than most districts, and they're just driving them crazy with all these calls. And a 2023 survey estimated that 30% of Medicare Advantage-eligible beneficiaries receive seven or more calls a week. I got to tell you, Mr. Chairman and witnesses, I've had constituents who have told me if they only got seven a day, they'd be thrilled. That would be a down number. So what can we do, because this is a huge issue in my district, what can we do to make that situation better?
Yeah, I think that those calls, if they're robocalls, if they're telemarketing calls, they may be in violation of the TCPA, they may be violation of the Telemarketing Sales Rule.

So how do we get them to use— because I've asked, I've said to folks as I've been talking with them, well, have you put yourself on the do not call list? And they say yes, but it doesn't seem to change anything. So how do we make that better?

So, one of the things is, and we'd be happy to work with you, we've got to traceback those calls. We have to see who is ignoring the law, get that information, get that to the right enforcement authorities to go after them. And we've seen success with that. Like, the auto warranty campaign was the same. We worked very closely with the states and the FCC, and that went from the most prolific robocall campaign in America to basically zero right now. So, that is that's the answer there.

All right. Well, I'd be glad to work with you anyway, because when I start going to events and I start hearing this at a majority of the events I go to, whether it be a street festival or a meeting of folks, that tells me we got a problem. Ms. Leggin, I got the toll texts.
Uh,

of course, I called my staff assistant and said, how come you haven't kept my account up to date? Not realizing I was on the road. And she said, it's a scam, don't worry about it. But I've gotten a number of those things since then and some others, and apparently somebody out there thinks I need a new job. And I click delete or report as junk and delete. Does that do any good?

It certainly does. That's one of the key tools that the wireless industry and our partners on the device side have made available for consumers to delete, report junk. You can also forward your scam text to 7726, which spells SPAM. And both of those are key inputs for wireless providers and our messaging partners in making our algorithms and filtering and blocking more sophisticated and responsive to what we're hearing from consumers out there like you and others in this room that have gotten those types of texts. In addition, we look at those types of scams, and we develop evidence on them and refer them to our law enforcement partners for investigation through our Secure Messaging Initiative as well, so that we're working to target the bad actors responsible.
All right, I appreciate that. Mr.—and I hope I get your name right—Waguespack.
Pretty good. Yeah.

All right, not too bad. Um, I don't know that I, I really have a question for you, but I'll just make a comment. As a recovering attorney, I hate the whole strike suit incident or industry where they get a niche and they just go after things. I want people to be able to sue when they're legitimately harmed. Um, and I just make the offer that if I can work with you in any way to try to make the law so that it, that it lets the legitimate complaint go forward but stops the strike suits where they're just trying to make it expensive and get a settlement— you, you talked about that earlier— just let me know what I can do to be of assistance. I will try.
I appreciate that. That's the balance we're looking for, and the balance is found in other federal statutes all across the code.
All right, I appreciate it. Yield back.
Thank you, Mr. Griffith. Next up is Mrs. Trahan.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Well, I'm glad to know that the frustration of unwanted robocalls is as universal in Congress as it is with our constituents. According to one estimate, Massachusetts residents received over 43 million robocalls in the month of May alone. Each of these unwanted calls wastes the precious time of the people we represent, and there are real risks that the caller on the other end is a scammer looking to swindle them out of hundreds or even thousands of dollars. The scourge of robocalls and robotexts must end, and yet the Trump administration does seem determined to cut enforcement agencies like the FCC and the FTC who fight for Americans every single day. Mr. Winters, can you just explain in brief the role that the FCC plays in combating robocalls and texts, and how how this agency works with private sector partners to do that?

Sure. Thanks for the question. The FCC has a lot of responsibility and a lot of a big thing to cover. But one of the things they do is maintain and establish the Robocall Mitigation Database. They have enforcement and investigation teams for reading consumer complaints, taking them in, analyzing it, and trying to do enforcement when possible. And I think they also work with industry colleagues, who maybe will speak more to that, to try to ensure that they are doing as much as they can. But I think that already, and even when there was no cuts to staffing, it's really hard for them to actually make meaningful consequences for the repeat bad actors, whether it's their inability to get the fines themselves or just the fact that there is a relatively low standard for the Robocall Mitigation Database. There are all sorts of reasons why, even if fully staffed, they don't quite have the right authorities or the right approach. And so, to cut their staffing would make it even harder.

Thank you. In February, President Trump signed the Executive Order 14215, incorrectly named Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies. This EO strips the independence from many of our regular regulatory agencies, including the FCC. And the FCC is essential in the fight against illegal robocalls, making the actions of the Trump administration all the more concerning. Mr. Winters, again, what effects will there be in the fight against illegal robocalls and texts if the Trump administration undermines the independence of federal agencies like the FCC?

Thanks. Yeah, the independent nature of the FCC and the FTC both is essential for them to be able to focus on consumer protection and not go down political pursuits. I highlighted a little bit in my oral and wrote more about it in my written testimony, but particularly at the FCC, this relationship with the White House has taken priority and makes it so Chairman Carr is most of the time talking about DEI hiring practices at companies and threatening to pull licenses for airing interviews with Democratic candidates, for example, as well as just focusing on providing contracts for people like Elon Musk and getting spectrum lines. All of that focus is not on consumer protection, right? And one of the reasons why is because of that lack of independence, where they can't focus on that because they're sort of focusing on the priorities of the president.

Thank you. The FCC's budget justification lists cracking down on illegal robocalls as a performance indicator for the agency, which is a necessary priority. Unfortunately, the Trump administration has doubled down on its mission to hamstring the federal government's ability to hold robocall scammers accountable by proposing to eliminate 74 positions at the FCC in the fiscal year 2026 budget. The FCC, however, is not alone in fighting robocalls. Industry has, in many instances, implemented solutions and voluntarily adopted best practices. Yes, they can always do more, but as lawmakers, we should look to build upon their good work while identifying gaps where the federal government can add value. Ms. Leggin, can you discuss the importance of public-private partnerships in combating robocalls and robotexts and suggest specific ways in which Congress can accelerate the efforts that industry has already taken?

Thank you. Public-private partnerships are a key tool in helping us go after bad actors so that we're stopping robocalls and robotexts at the source. CTIA's members participate in the U.S. Telecom Industry Traceback Group to help identify the bad actors behind illegal robocalls. And our members on the wireless side and then also throughout the messaging ecosystem participate in CTIA's Secure Messaging Initiative, which convenes the messaging ecosystem to share information among each other and with our law enforcement partners across the federal agencies and with the State Attorney General Enforcement Task Force so that they can take that information and go after the bad actors as well.
Thank you. Thank you to all the witnesses. I appreciate it.
Thank you. Next up is the gentleman from Pennsylvania, Dr. Joyce.

Thank you, Chairman and Ranking Member, for holding today's hearing, and thank you for all of the witnesses who have agreed to testify today. When I return to my district, Pennsylvania's 13th Congressional District, I hear about the pervasive and unrelenting illegal robocalls and texts that my constituents are faced with, often on a daily basis. So many of my constituents are senior citizens. I sat down and did a senior citizen seminar twice in the district in the last month, and you hear recurrent themes. You hear the, Grandma, Grandma, it's Mike. I'm in Mexico and I'm in jail. I need your help. I need it. It sounded just like Mike. I hear that repeatedly when I have these roundtable discussions with seniors. And it seems like the scammers are getting creative and finding actually new ways to trick us with incredible-looking text messages and very convincing grandma and grandpa calls. Scammers have even learned how to incorporate AI into intimidating loved ones to convince them to turn over personal information—credit card numbers, bank numbers. Too many of my constituents are risking their retirement savings, and subsequently they lose faith in the system that we have set in place to protect them. We need to do better. We need to both educate consumers and anticipate the next angle of attack that these scammers will take, particularly with the assistance of our partners in law enforcement and the DOJ. Mr. Bercu, your testimony mentioned a project piloted by the Industry Traceback Group, ITG, in partnership with banks and carriers aimed at tackling fraud and consumer financial losses. Can you elaborate on the pilot goals and successes thus far, and is there collaboration with law enforcement?

Yeah, absolutely. I, I think some of the most promising work our industry is doing is partnering across sectors because it, it the, the fraudsters are hurting our collective customers, whether that's banks or, or the carriers and your constituents. So what we've been doing is working with banks to help them identify where their number has been spoofed in a few carriers. So working with the carriers, getting examples of calls that the carriers see from the bank's number, getting that back to the bank, and the bank can tell us, oh, those weren't us. And we're— what we're doing with that is 2 things. We're able to trace that back Find out who made the calls, find out where this— who was spoofing the number, get that information in the hands of law enforcement to take action with it, but also help the bank identify and look at those customers and say, oh, did any of these customers that got the fake call pretending to be us have a suspicious transaction, and helping to find that. And I think criminal enforcement has to be a key here because that's— we know the scammers will use any tool available to them, and they won't stop just because it gets a little harder. They keep evolving. And so the key is going after them, and we stand ready to continue to support that.

And I agree, the scammers certainly have the ability to be incredibly crafty, devious, and downright evil in this regard. Talk to me about how you interface with financial institutions to make them aware of these situations.

So, I think that's actually one of the promising things going on across the industry is that we work directly with a lot of the financial institutions. We work with tech companies, others. Marriott was mentioned before. We worked very closely with Marriott to trace the calls purporting to be Marriott. So that's what we're doing, but there's broader conversations now about how how the industries can even keep growing and continue to integrate. In my opening testimony, one thing I mentioned I think Congress can do to help here is a safe harbor for that fraud information sharing because I think there are questions about rules and risks when you do share information. So I think that's one way we can continue to unlock those good partnerships.

And thank you. Thank you for being proactive in this. Mr. Waguespack, many of my constituents are in rural central Pennsylvania, where internet connectivity is difficult and educational digital resources on illegal robocalls are inaccessible. How can federal agencies and industry partner, coordinate efforts to better educate consumers, specifically in rural areas with limited internet access and those digital resources?

Well, I think, on leaning into what has been done since TCPA was first initiated, where you have private-sector solutions going in and working with—we've talked a lot about FCC and FTC, but also the local law enforcement and local financial institutions on the ground there, putting that initiative out there. Mr. Bercu talked about some of the information sharing that are done with the banks to prevent the fraud. There's also a second level down. It's a good example of the education program. Through the Bankers Association, they've armed about 2,000 banks out there to talk to their consumers. Here's a hit list of the things we will never ask you for, so if you get an email that has this, this, this, or this, ignore it, it's spam. Here's how you call us back. And so we can use the private sector, I think, to develop some of that messaging and make sure consumers can be informed of the decisions they need to be able to fight back on their own.
I thank all of the witnesses for presenting here today. Mr. Chairman, my time has expired, and I yield back.
Thank you. Next up is the gentlelady from Texas, Ms. Fletcher.

Well, thank you and thanks to our Chairman Palmer and Ranking Member Clarke for convening this hearing today. Thank you to our witnesses for all of your testimony. I think it's been really helpful for all of us, and as we've heard throughout the morning, abusive robocalls and robotexts are not just nuisance, right? They're danger, and we need to do something about that. I appreciate the work that you are doing and also the issues that you've brought to our attention this morning and the conversation around what we can do about it. And I am concerned, as several of my colleagues have mentioned, that we're hearing consistently from you we need more enforcement, we need more coordination, we need adequate resourcing, and we need adequate staffing to be able to do some of the things we're doing in a complex and challenging environment where the technology is moving faster than Congress, faster than our agencies, and what we're seeing at the same time is that those resources, both in terms of money and staff, are being cut from the administration as we speak. They are asking Congress to rescind additional funding. They're stopping funding. And so, as several of my colleagues have noted, agencies like the FCC, the FTC, and the DOJ have actually utilized the law that we passed together, the work that we've done collaboratively to understand the problems and really conduct meaningful enforcement that has stopped scammers. And now it seems like the administration is taking the cops off the beat in this area and in many others. Mr. Winters, you noted in your testimony and you mentioned just earlier this morning that the Trump administration has taken steps to dissolve the DOJ's Consumer Protection Bureau. And I believe you just said the Consumer Protection Branch of the DOJ. You just told us this morning that they had successfully prosecuted a case and stopped scammers who had— I guess it was against the data brokers who had sold the data of 30 million Americans. And that data winds up in the hands of criminals who use it in these scams and others. So I think it's really important that we understand that these agencies need to be fully funded and that shuttering something like the DOJ's Consumer Protection Branch, this expert-led enforcement agency, really puts our communities at more risk. It's not something we should be doing. You also mentioned in your testimony the CFPB, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and the work that it has done in this area, and the administration is also shuttering or attempting to shutter that agency that Congress created and that has been really critical to protecting consumers. And that's what we're talking about in this hearing: protecting consumers, protecting American citizens from these scams. I think that what we're hearing this morning also calls on all of us on this committee to redouble our efforts to do our work around creating comprehensive privacy laws that protect American consumers, because what I'm hearing from you and what we're seeing is that our data is being stolen, is being sold, is being used, and it's being used by these scammers. So can you take, with the time that we have, just can you talk a little bit more about cutting the DOJ's Consumer Protection Branch as well as the CFPB and what that would mean, Mr. Winters, in terms of protecting American consumers in this larger context? If you want to talk, too, about just the effort to take away the staff and the funding for these agencies that are protecting consumers from robocalls and robotexts that we're all clearly worried about and clearly concerned we want to address, how is this going to help or hurt us in that effort?

Yeah, absolutely. And thank you for the question. Very simply, taking resources away from these agencies, and in the case of the CFPB and this part of the DOJ, completely trying to stop all of their work is absolutely not going to help in the fight against these harms. On the DOJ Consumer Protection case that I mentioned, yeah, that is a data broker that sold a list of over 30 million elderly Americans directly to a scammer. It's not just that it ended up in the scammer's hands. Data brokers will sell to anyone at any time. And so what Congress needs to do for both scam reasons and lots of other reasons is pass comprehensive data privacy law with data minimization and private right of action and a few other key things. Or at least if you want to be more focused, it should be focused on restricting the sale of consumer data. CFPB specifically, the shuttering that really cuts off an essential resource for people that are victims of scams especially. They have had counselors, people that answer the phone and take complaints and try to get things resolved for you. There's a bunch of great stories of people that had literally had their scams resolved. They got money back from their bank with the help of CFPB professionals. So they can do things on enforcement and work with financial actors where people are losing their money, but they also are just critical support. And they provide also tracking of those complaints and gets it to state AGs and those who can help.
Well, thank you, Mr. Winters. I've gone over my time. I do have more questions for the panel, so I will submit them for the record, and I will yield back. Thank you.
Thank you. Next up is Mr. Tonko.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Americans received over 52 billion robocalls in 2024, which is nearly 200 calls for every American adult. Americans also have lost $25 billion annually to scams that begin as spam calls. Unfortunately, we know that scammers often target older Americans who are especially vulnerable victims to these scams. Older adults, in particular, lost $4.9 billion through all types of fraud last year alone. I know I listened to the exchange that you had with my colleague Representative DeGette, but I want to delve into this with the senior perspective. Certain scams put even the most technical-savvy at risk, scams that, in some cases, mimic law enforcement, hospitals, or Medicare, or the voices of family members seeming to be in danger or in need of money. So Mr. Winters, what specific tactics do scammers use to target seniors and other vulnerable groups?

Yeah, I mean, and thank you for the question. Scammers in general capitalize on uncertainty and fear, and especially for seniors, especially those who are on a fixed income, all sorts of concerns about an unpaid bill, a toll account that you don't quite have set up yet, Medicare, you know, potential fraud and targeting, like, they are going to be thinking that the senior citizens are good targets for it. This is exactly why we had the case where a data broker bought a large list of senior citizens and targeted them with scams. And that's, you know, a terrible thing. And so, again, yeah, they try to capitalize on uncertainty and fear. And that's why you see lost bills. Job opportunities, especially in this current climate where a lot of people are getting fired and the economic uncertainty is everywhere, the job opportunity scams are going to be— more people are going to fall for them because it's, you know, You want a job. You need a job. You need to pay your bills. So, you know, I think that those are some of the ways in which they are targeting everyone, but, you know, are hitting seniors most.
And what prevention strategies have been the most successful in that fight against illegal robocalls and texts?

Yeah. So, you know, there have been really strong enforcement actions by the Federal Trade Commission of voice-over-internet providers. So, you know, I think the most appropriate and effective enforcement is going sort of upstream, especially when you are trying to get accountability for some of the actors that are providing the content or the delivery or the targets of some of these scams. One other really good case was the Rytr case by the FTC last year where they targeted using the means and instrumentalities concept. In this case, it was a a tool that generated lots of fake reviews, and the FTC was cracking down on fake reviews. But you can use that same tool to generate sort of an endless list of scam texts. And that sort of, you know, is a force multiplier for scammers. And again, you know, the the use of these AI tools makes it harder because, you know, there's no typos. It comes in, you know, perfect English, and there's no, you know, these weird links that we've all sort of become accustomed to. So that makes it even tougher.
Thank you. And Ms. Leggin, how is the wireless industry working to protect that older community and otherwise more vulnerable customers?

That's a priority for the wireless industry. And to do that, we work with AARP and we support their National Elder Fraud Coordination Center, which works to take reports of victim losses in and then bring cases against bad actors. We also were happy to participate in the FTC's Stop Senior Scams Working Group, and we led the working group focused on text messaging issues, which was a cross-sector effort to explore ways that we could do more to protect older Americans from scams. We also participate in other working groups with consumers directly to try to push out our educational materials so that they know which texts not to click on, which calls not to answer. And we have those resources on our website and our members' websites as well.

Thank you. And the AARP that you mentioned has said that, I quote, "The alarmingly high levels of fraud against older adults underscores that stronger protections are urgently needed." So as technology evolves, so must our ability to combat these illegal and harmful calls and texts. Mr. Bercu, what additional tools does the Industry Traceback Group need to protect Americans from fraudulent calls or fraudulent texts?

Thank you for the question. So I mentioned in my opening testimony, I think there's ways to build on what's working and reinvest in our work. We are always adapting to the threat. A few years ago, we were only really tracing illegal robocalls. Now we're tracing threatening calls, we're tracing targeted scams, and I think that doubled last year, how many we traced. So we're always adapting, and I think Congress's support on through targeted immunity, through extending the cycle, will allow us to continue to invest and innovate.
Well, I thank you very much, and with that, I yield back.
Thank you. Next up is the gentlelady from New York, Ocasio-Cortez, please.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Mr. Winters, I want folks back home to kind of understand why this problem is happening. The average American receives about 15 robocalls each month, but obviously, depending on who you are, you could be experiencing that in a day. And we know that it wasn't always like this. So, I want folks to understand what the root of this problem is so that they also understand what some of our solutions can be. Is it fair to say that essentially back in the day, calls used to be routed through phone wires, through your telecom company. And so your telecom provider, whether it was Verizon or AT&T or T-Mobile, they were responsible for routing the calls, and therefore they were kind of able to trace who was making them. Is that right?
Uh, yes.

And then as internet applications started to grow, then voice service providers and calls over digital services started to really expand in their infrastructure. And so it wasn't just your, your cell phone provider or your even your landline provider that was in charge of your phone calls. It then became kind of these other kind of internet companies, right?
Yeah, there's a lot of intermediary service providers. Sometimes a call will go through 8 or 10 of them before reaching you through AT&T or whatever.

Yeah, so that it is, it was really in that switch from from call and telecom providers to the expanding growth of internet providers that really kind of allowed the volume of these calls to blossom? Because we weren't just talking about telecom regulation, but internet regulation, right?
I think that's definitely a lot of the reason to blame for those additional intermediary providers that are harder to track through.

And so it's not it's no longer about who your personal provider is. As you said, you could have 8, you could have 10 of these companies routing this call. So you have the person who wants to make this robocall, and then it just leapfrogs between all these intermediary companies. Mr. Winters, how many of these intermediary companies currently exist, and does the government have any way to keep track of who these actors are?

Thanks for the question. Yeah, it is kind of an unanswerable question. I think it's probably since we've been there, there's probably additional companies that have popped up and registered on the Robocall Mitigation Database. I think last time I checked a few days ago, it was over 9,500 of these intermediary service providers. And so, there is a list online. It is not a high barrier to entry. You have to register that you are a company, you have to put a robocall mitigation plan in the form, but there's not a lot of vetting there, right?

Yeah. And if these kind of abusive companies, sure, they have to register, but if we find that they're not complying, the consequence just seems to be that they get delisted from the database, correct?
Only sometimes. Not even that sometimes.
Okay.
Yeah.
And, and, but without any additional penalties, is there anything to stop these companies from just immediately getting relisted?
No, you can, you know, if you are delisted, you can get another corporation and set it up and sign up again.

So if you're a bad actor in this space, someone that's really perpetuating spam calls, in some cases fraudulent calls, you can be found to be breaking these rules, you can get delisted from the FCC, and then you could just turn around and it's, what, a hundred bucks to—
I think that's not even necessarily enforced yet, but yeah, it'll be $100.

Yeah, it's $100, and maybe you'll have to pay it, maybe not. Um, so clearly there's an enforcement problem here on keeping these these bad actors out of the space. Um, in your opinion as a consumer protection advocate, how can we as Congress work to strengthen some of these protections, and what do you think some of the best solutions here are?

Yeah, I think particularly to the lack of accountability in the Robocall Mitigation Database, there's a few really easy things that either the FCC can do or Congress can instruct the FCC to do to speed that up, I guess. There is a really low barrier of Right now, you have to have reasonable precautions of taking to mitigate robocalls, and that standard should be increased to effective actual implementation. There should be requirements for the downstream providers, the bigger companies, to have responsibility for the calls that they're taking in from those 8 to 10, whatever, plus intermediary service providers. And there is just insufficient tracking, insufficient consequences for repeat offenders, even even under the the company they're doing. And one thing that we advocate for to try to increase that accountability, 'cause it is genuinely a difficult problem to try to track all these service providers, even if there's a full-court press. But one proposal we've put out there is to implement bonding for Robocall Mitigation Database members, so that a third party is incentivized to make sure that they're actually doing what they say they're going to do and help protect consumers. So, very happy to work with your office to try to make that happen. Thanks.
Thank you very much. I yield back.
Next up is Mr. Mullin for five minutes.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you all for being here today. Americans lose billions of dollars every year to phone-based scams. We must crack down on illegal robocalls and robotexts. With the recent enactment of laws that further empower enforcement agencies, there has been progress toward protecting people from these predatory practices, but not enough. I want to recognize former Congresswoman Anna Eshoo, who represents a district neighboring mine. She's represented that for over 30 years before her recent retirement. I want to thank her for her leadership on this issue. She introduced key legislation like the HANG UP Act and the Robocalls and Texts Act, and I'm proud to help uplift some of that work that she led on in this committee and hopefully carry it forward in the future. As we've heard today, more must be done to keep up with the rapidly advancing technology and the increasingly sophisticated tactics that scammers are using. Enforcement agencies need the tools and resources to stay ahead. The more sophisticated the methods, the more likely people fall victim to them. As more companies integrate AI into their products, it's becoming even harder for consumers to distinguish legitimate communication from fraud. Mr. Bercu, you mentioned AI-generated messages are harder to detect and can present challenges for enforcement. How can the government and industry better coordinate to establish safeguards to limit harm to people from illegal calls using AI?

Thank you for the question. I think the fact that the criminal actors behind these calls use AI just underscores they will use every tool, every channel available to them to defraud Americans. And I think that's one of the challenges we have, is they're already violating the law with impunity. They're committing fraud. That's violation of the criminal code. So that's one of the things I think we think, is we do need a national strategy. We do need to prioritize criminal enforcement because they're going to continue to use the tools. And from the carrier perspective, there's not going to be a good way to know which tools they're using because, as Mr. Winters pointed out, they're so far upstream from where our members sit.

Thank you for that. We know that certain people in our communities are particularly vulnerable, like seniors and individuals with limited English proficiency. Mr. Winters, what can the FTC, in coordination with other agencies, do to be proactive in protecting vulnerable populations from these kinds of scams?

for the question. I think it is a lot of the same of working to cut off the problem at the source, right? So whether we're talking about an AI tool that makes it super easy to generate a million texts that threaten to be immigration enforcement or something, for example, the enforcement action should target those developers that are putting those products out there. Same thing goes for putting liability and responsibility for people throughout the call stream to make sure that the calls they're taking content from are actually doing what they're saying they're going to do. But I think that the FTC and all these state attorneys general as well can be doing more to do better investigation of the members of the Robocall Mitigation Database, making sure that the STIR/SHAKEN protocols are implemented thoroughly and actually does what it's supposed to do. I think a lot of times we see scam calls that have the high level of attestation, despite that being the whole point. So I think that there's just a lot more that they can do together.

So how are those agency cuts going to hinder FTC's ability to advance its efforts to combat illegal robocalls and robotexts?

It will hurt their ability to do so. As we've talked about, it's already a really difficult issue, even if you are trying your best and have all the resources you can. If you are taking people away, especially of an agency like the FTC that has a really broad jurisdiction, of course you're going to have less resources, less creative cases, just because more things are being put on less people,
uh,

and the priorities aren't there, uh, either. And so, especially without the commissioners, Uh, the 2 of the— 2 of the 5 commissioners, you don't get dissent, you don't get the conversations that might generate more creative ideas or different ideas. Uh, and so between that and the staffing, uh, it will just make it a lot harder.
Thank you for that. I yield back.
Thank you. Next up is the gentleman from Texas, Mr. Pfluger.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thanks for the witnesses being here. I want to take a little bit different approach on this and just talk about a little bit of the impact that I'm not sure has been fully discussed today, and that is to physicians. And I'm in the process of getting screenshots of the physicians in my district, and one in particular who is showing me kind of the impact of about 20 a day that they're getting that is really preventing these calls. And so I took a I just wrote down from the screenshot the calls that recently came in. This was from last week on Friday: 2:31, 2:53, 2:57, 3:48, 3:53, 3:58, 3:59, 4:38, and 4:48. And in that period of time, starting at 2:30, ending at almost 5:00 p.m., there were a number of patients that were disrupted. So I know we're beating a dead horse with just how how painful these things are, but that actually is pretty serious when they can't take a call from the labor and delivery section saying, Hey, we have an incident here that you need to get up pretty quick and deliver. So I'll start with Ms. Leggin. And by the way, thank y'all. I know we're all working together to try to solve these. But to what extent do you see TCPA and TRACED being effective? And then I'll go a step further. We've had these discussions already in this hearing, but the sense of urgency and what else needs to be done to prevent that physician and all the other physicians from having to deal with that in the middle of what could be an emergency situation?

Thank you for the question, and that it seems like a serious issue. TRACED and the TCPA are great tools that are helpful in helping bring enforcement actions against bad actors under the TCPA if you're violating those consent, autodialer, prerecorded voice provisions. But unfortunately, bad actors don't care about the TCPA or other laws, so they're going to spam you no matter what. And that's where our work with law enforcement partnerships on the calling side through the ITG or on the texting side through the Secure Messaging Initiative to bring investigations against those bad actors so that we're stopping those at the source are really helpful.
Yeah, go ahead.

And I was just going to say, to support those efforts further, you know, you've heard me say throughout this hearing, we, we would welcome help from Congress in prioritizing resources towards enforcement to bring more cases against those bad actors.

What do you think we can do— and anybody's open to answer this— what do you think we can do for hospitals in general You know, for those that are providing emergency services, because nobody's using a pager anymore. It's all cell phone. Maybe they need to go back to that. But what can we do, you know, to think creatively to really stop that for those— I mean, every constituent of mine wants it stopped, but are there specific ideas?

That's a good question. You know, it's a really challenging issue, especially when we want to make sure that critical public safety public health services need to get their calls through.
